answer_text:
Let

\[
A(x)=\int_0^x |f'(t)|^2\,dt.
\]

Then \(A(0)=0\), \(A(1)=\int_0^1 |f'(t)|^2\,dt\le 1\), and since \(f\) is continuously differentiable,

\[
A'(x)=|f'(x)|^2.
\]

For each \(x\in[0,1]\), using \(f(0)=0\),

\[
|f(x)|=\left|\int_0^x f'(t)\,dt\right|
\le \int_0^x |f'(t)|\,dt.
\]

By Cauchy–Schwarz,

\[
\int_0^x |f'(t)|\,dt
\le \sqrt{x}\left(\int_0^x |f'(t)|^2\,dt\right)^{1/2}
= \sqrt{x}\,A(x)^{1/2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{|f(x)|}{\sqrt{x}}\le A(x)^{1/2}.
\]

Hence the given integral satisfies

\[
\int_0^1 |f'(x)|^2\frac{|f(x)|}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx
\le \int_0^1 A'(x)A(x)^{1/2}\,dx.
\]

But

\[
\int_0^1 A'(x)A(x)^{1/2}\,dx
= \int_0^1 \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{2}{3}A(x)^{3/2}\right)\,dx
= \frac{2}{3}A(1)^{3/2}.
\]

Since \(A(1)\le 1\),

\[
\int_0^1 |f'(x)|^2\frac{|f(x)|}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx
\le \frac{2}{3}.
\]

This bound is attained by \(f(x)=x\). Indeed,

\[
\int_0^1 |f'(x)|^2\frac{|f(x)|}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx
= \int_0^1 1\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx
= \int_0^1 x^{1/2}\,dx
= \frac{2}{3}.
\]

Thus the maximum value is

\[
\boxed{\frac{2}{3}}.
\]
